title: One fine night
hook: don't chase the past, don't pin hopes on the future; see what is here, today

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yama's questions, and your line, the messengers came. Did a baby or an elder carry a message to you? Today, a short verse that answers it. Day four hundred ninety-nine.

Ten minutes in old photos pulls the mood one way. Ten minutes planning next year pulls it another. Two very different moods, and in both of them, the room you're sitting in has gone missing. The hundred and thirty-first discourse is short, and at its heart is a verse of just a few lines. The Buddha recites it at Jeta's Grove near Savatthi, then explains it. And it won't stay in one discourse: the next three come back to it. Today: bhaddekaratta.
screen: `TEN MINUTES IN OLD PHOTOS.` → `TEN MINUTES IN NEXT YEAR.` → `A SHORT VERSE, EXPLAINED.`

segments.voice: Here's what the verse says, in paraphrase. Don't chase after the past. Don't build your hopes on the future. The past is already left behind. The future hasn't come. Whatever is present, see it clearly, right where it is, steady and unshaken. Do today what needs doing with energy. Who knows, death may come tomorrow, and there's no bargaining with death and his great army. Whoever lives this way, keen, day and night, the peaceful sage calls one who has had a bhaddekaratta. And what is that word? Bhadda means good or auspicious. Eka means one. Ratta is the hard part: it's usually read as night, but translators don't agree on the whole, so you'll find one fine night, a single excellent night, or an auspicious day. What's clear is the shape of the teaching. Then the Buddha explains how people chase the past: thinking, I had such a body, such feelings, such thoughts, and finding delight there. How they build hopes on the future: I'll have such a body, such feelings. And how, in the present, they take body or feeling or mind as a self, and get pulled along. The one who doesn't is the one having that fine night. Not a night of special visions. A night, or a day, lived where it actually is. After yesterday's messengers, this is the answer: not fear, but full attention to the only day there is.
screen: `DON'T CHASE THE PAST` · `DON'T PIN HOPES ON THE FUTURE` · `SEE WHAT IS HERE, TODAY` · `BHADDA, EKA, RATTA` · then, large: `ONE FINE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: live one day this way. Start now, for two minutes. Sit, and each time the mind slides into a memory, say softly: past. Each time it jumps to a plan, say: future. Then come back to what's actually here: this breath, this sound, this weight. You don't have to hate the past or the future. You're just choosing, for now, the room you're in. The bell holds the time.
Bhaddekaratta. One fine night, an auspicious day: not chasing the past, not hoping on the future, seeing what's here clearly, today. Today's word.
Your line: one fine night. Today, catch yourself once in old photos and once in next year, and come back to the room you're actually in. Day four hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: The bhaddekaratta verse is chanted in some Theravada monasteries, and meditation teachers in several traditions use it to teach dwelling in the present moment.

fork.setup: you've caught yourself delighting in how things used to be. what does the Buddha's explanation call that?
fork.reveal: thinking 'I had such a body, such feelings' and finding delight there is reviving the past, in the Buddha's explanation.

original.note: Pali bhaddekaratta: bhadda, good; eka, one; ratta, perhaps night. its exact sense is debated.

trapdoor: what you thought: one fine night means a lovely evening out.
what it means: a day and night lived fully in the present, not chasing the past or the future.
what a scholar hears: translators render bhaddekaratta differently, and the verse returns in the next three discourses, MN 132 to 134, with different speakers.
